title: OpenAI and Anthropic Turn to Consulting Firms to Help Businesses Adopt AI
author: David Adubiina

dom.t: AI services: Deployment gaps create consulting opportunity

st.t: AI services: Deployment gaps create consulting opportunity
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that enterprise AI deployment gaps create a professional-services opportunity. It reports limited scaling and financial benefits, then presents consulting partnerships, forward-deployed engineers, workflow integration and process redesign as the proposed response, while appropriately stopping short of claiming demonstrated results.
qs: The partnerships aim to address a widening gap between the promise of AI and how widely companies actually use it.
Consulting firms are expected to help shape strategy and redesign business processes around the tools.

kp.k: AI developers enlist consultants to support enterprise deployment
kp.d: The article reports, citing The Wall Street Journal, that OpenAI and Anthropic are partnering with consulting firms to help corporate clients integrate AI into operations and move beyond experimentation. Named consulting firms include McKinsey, Boston Consulting Group, Accenture, Capgemini and Deloitte. This is evidence about enterprise AI adoption and consulting, rather than legal services directly.
qs: Artificial intelligence companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are increasingly partnering with consulting firms to help businesses deploy AI tools, as many organisations struggle to move beyond early experiments with the technology.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, the companies have struck agreements with consulting firms including McKinsey, Boston Consulting Group, Accenture, Capgemini and Deloitte to help corporate clients integrate AI systems into their operations.

kp.k: Surveys indicate limited scaling and reported financial benefits
kp.d: A McKinsey survey of nearly 2,000 employees conducted 'last summer' found about two-thirds reporting that their organisations had not begun enterprise-wide AI scaling. Separately, a PricewaterhouseCoopers survey of nearly 4,500 chief executives found more than half reporting little or no financial benefit so far. These are respondents' reports of adoption and benefits, not direct measurements of AI performance.
qs: A McKinsey survey of nearly 2,000 employees last summer found that about two-thirds said their organisations had not yet begun scaling AI across the enterprise.
In a separate survey of nearly 4,500 chief executives conducted by PricewaterhouseCoopers, more than half reported seeing little or no financial benefit from AI so far.

kp.k: Deployment combines engineering support with business-process redesign
kp.d: The article describes OpenAI's Frontier platform as enabling businesses to build and manage task-specific AI agents. Citing the Journal, it reports roughly 70 forward-deployed engineers working with organisations to identify use cases and integrate technology into workflows, while consultants are expected to shape strategy and redesign processes. OpenAI's Colin Jarvis reports that a large European bank evaluated potential Frontier applications in credit-risk analysis and voice capabilities; the example concerns evaluation, not demonstrated deployment results.
qs: To close that gap, OpenAI has been working with consulting firms to help companies deploy its Frontier platform, which allows businesses to build and manage AI agents for specific tasks.

The company’s team of roughly 70 forward-deployed engineers works directly with organisations to identify potential use cases and integrate the technology into real-world workflows, the Journal reported.
Consulting firms are expected to help shape strategy and redesign business processes around the tools.

At a large European bank, OpenAI and one of its consulting partners evaluated several potential uses for Frontier, including applications related to credit-risk analysis and voice capabilities, Colin Jarvis, OpenAI’s global head of forward-deployed engineering, told the Journal.

kp.k: Anthropic partnerships target industry-specific AI solutions
kp.d: The article reports that Anthropic announced a Deloitte partnership 'last year' to develop industry-specific AI solutions and also works with other consulting firms. Separately, Bill Achtmeyer characterises firms as seeking advantageous alliances with AI companies; his statement is an industry interpretation, not evidence of exclusive arrangements.
qs: The company announced a partnership with Deloitte last year to develop industry-specific AI solutions and also works with other consulting firms.

“All the firms are tying themselves up with one or the other, trying to figure out who’s best to be with,” Bill Achtmeyer, chairman at Acropolis Advisors and founder of strategy consulting firm Parthenon, told the Journal.

kp.k: Breadth of AI applications creates demand for consulting
kp.d: The article reports analysts' view that the broad range of possible AI applications drives consulting demand. K2 Consulting Research's Tom Rodenhauser argues that AI differs from earlier technological advances because applications are broad and many potential uses remain undiscovered. This is an attributed explanation of demand rather than a quantified causal finding.
qs: Industry analysts say the broad range of possible AI applications is driving demand for consulting services.

“AI stands apart from previous tech advances because its applications are so broad, and many potential uses have yet to be discovered,” Tom Rodenhauser, managing partner at K2 Consulting Research, told the Journal.

kp.k: Consulting growth accompanies rising AI-related bookings
kp.d: The article presents growing AI-related work as boosting consulting. K2 Consulting Research estimates global consulting revenue grew 5.5 per cent in 2025, roughly double the previous year's rate. Accenture reported $2.2 billion in new AI-related bookings in its most recent quarter, up $400 million from the prior quarter. The global figure concerns overall consulting revenue, whereas Accenture's figure concerns AI-related bookings.
qs: The surge in AI-related work is already boosting the consulting sector.
K2 Consulting Research estimates global consulting revenue grew 5.5 per cent in 2025, roughly double the rate recorded the previous year.
Accenture, for example, reported $2.2 billion in new AI-related bookings in its most recent quarter, an increase of $400 million from the prior quarter.

kp.k: Some consulting firms shift toward outcome-based pricing
kp.d: Citing the Journal, the article reports that some consulting firms are moving toward payment tied to achieving specified results rather than consulting-team size. Rodenhauser predicts a dramatic change to the consulting model known over the last 50 years. The reported shift is qualified as affecting some firms; its prevalence and results are not quantified.
qs: According to the journal, some firms are shifting toward outcome-based pricing models where they are paid based on whether projects achieve specific results rather than the size of consulting teams involved.
“The way we’ve known consulting over the last 50 years changes pretty dramatically,” Rodenhauser said.

kp.k: Human accountability may sustain demand for strategic advisers
kp.d: The article reports some analysts' expectation that companies will continue relying on human advisers for major strategic decisions. Shine Capital founder Mo Koyfman frames this demand as a desire for an identifiable human whom clients can contact and hold responsible when things go wrong. This is a prediction and interpretation, not a measured finding about client behaviour.
qs: Still, some analysts say companies will continue to rely on human advisers when making major strategic decisions.
As Mo Koyfman, founder of venture capital firm Shine Capital, put it: “They want a throat to cchoke… They want to be able to pick up a phone and call a human being and say, ‘You screwed me.’”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Adubiina reports that AI developers are increasingly using consulting partnerships to help corporate clients move from experiments to operational deployment.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain article about enterprise AI adoption and consulting, not legal services. Drawing on The Wall Street Journal, Adubiina reports agreements involving OpenAI, Anthropic, McKinsey, Boston Consulting Group, Accenture, Capgemini and Deloitte. He describes consultants' expected contribution as strategy and business-process redesign, alongside technical integration by OpenAI's forward-deployed engineers. The partnerships are presented as a response to adoption difficulties, not as proof that those difficulties have been overcome.

pts.k: Tom Rodenhauser argues that AI's unusually broad and still partly undiscovered applications create demand for consulting services.
pts.d: Adubiina attributes the demand explanation to industry analysts, with Rodenhauser of K2 Consulting Research supplying the explicit rationale. Bill Achtmeyer separately describes consulting firms as competing to align with AI developers. These are attributed industry interpretations rather than measured estimates of the causal effect of application breadth on demand.

pts.k: Adubiina claims AI-related work is already boosting consulting, while some firms are moving toward payment for results rather than team size.
pts.d: The article connects consulting-sector growth and Accenture's AI bookings to rising AI work. It also reports, via The Wall Street Journal, a shift by some firms toward outcome-based pricing. Rodenhauser predicts a dramatic change in the established consulting model. The pricing claim is qualified as applying to some firms, not the whole industry; the growth figures do not separately quantify AI's contribution to total consulting revenue.

pts.k: The article presents continued reliance on human strategic advisers as a qualification to AI-driven change, with Mo Koyfman emphasising personal accountability.
pts.d: Adubiina reports that some analysts expect companies to retain human advisers for major strategic decisions. Koyfman's quoted explanation is that clients want a human they can contact and hold responsible when advice goes wrong. This is an expectation about enduring client preferences, not evidence that all consulting tasks will remain human-delivered.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Two reported surveys support the article's account of limited enterprise scaling and limited realised financial benefits.
pts.d: A McKinsey survey of nearly 2,000 employees reportedly found that about two-thirds said their organisations had not begun enterprise-wide scaling. A separate PwC survey of nearly 4,500 CEOs reportedly found that more than half had seen little or no financial benefit so far. These are respondents' reports, not direct measurements of deployment or financial returns. The article provides no further methodology and no survey evidence that consulting partnerships resolve the reported problems.

pts.k: Reported partnerships, an engineering team and a bank use-case assessment illustrate the deployment model, without documenting successful outcomes.
pts.d: Adubiina reports that OpenAI uses its Frontier platform and roughly 70 forward-deployed engineers to support integration. Colin Jarvis, OpenAI's global head of forward-deployed engineering, supplies the example of a large European bank where OpenAI and a consulting partner evaluated potential credit-risk and voice applications. Anthropic's Deloitte partnership is another example. The bank case concerns evaluation of possible uses, not a completed deployment with measured benefits.

pts.k: The commercial-growth claim draws on a consulting revenue estimate and Accenture's reported AI bookings; pricing and human-accountability claims rely on reporting and expert opinion.
pts.d: K2 Consulting Research estimates 5.5% global consulting revenue growth in 2025, roughly twice the preceding year's rate. Accenture reports $2.2 billion in new AI-related bookings in its most recent quarter, up $400 million quarter on quarter. Bookings are distinct from revenue, and the sector-wide revenue figure is not limited to AI work. No named outcome-priced project, measured prevalence of that pricing model, or systematic evidence of clients' accountability preferences is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes changes underway around its 2026 publication, with dated growth evidence but no firm deadline for broader transformation.
pts.d: Consulting revenue growth is explicitly for 2025 versus the previous year. The McKinsey survey is dated only as 'last summer', and Anthropic's Deloitte partnership as 'last year', both relative to the article's 2026 date. Accenture's quarter is not identified by calendar or fiscal period; the PwC survey is also undated. Scaling and financial-benefit shortfalls are qualified by 'not yet' and 'so far'. Future transformation has no specified completion date. Outcome-based pricing applies to some firms, while continued human reliance is specifically associated with major strategic decisions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are enterprise buyers, AI developers, consulting firms and human advisers; the source makes no legal-market-specific claim.
pts.d: Corporate clients receive help identifying uses, integrating tools and redesigning workflows, with a large European bank as the concrete example. OpenAI and Anthropic use consulting relationships to support adoption of their systems. Consulting firms gain AI-related demand and may face changes in project design and remuneration. Forward-deployed engineers perform technical integration, while human advisers are expected to retain an accountability role in major decisions. Deloitte appears as a consulting partner and PwC as a survey source, not as evidence about Big Four legal-service delivery. The article makes no claim about lawyers, law-firm staffing, legal clients or access to justice.
